read: full: abstract, sections 1-6 and impact statement (pp. 1-10) in full; appendix B.1 (LLM-as-judge on Hugging Face models, Figure 8) and the full regressions skimmed
venue_now: ICML 2025, PMLR 267 (page 1 footer: 'Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada'); arXiv 2506.07962v1, 9 Jun 2025
what_it_is: A large-scale measurement of how correlated LLM errors are. Using per-question answers of 349 LLMs on 12,032 multiple-choice questions (Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard), 71 LLMs on 14,042 MMLU questions (HELM) and 20 LLMs rating 1,800 resume-job pairs, it measures how often two models give the same wrong answer when both err. Errors are strongly correlated (mean agreement when both are wrong 0.423 on Hugging Face against a 0.127 random baseline, 0.6 on HELM against 1/3), more so for models from the same company, with the same base architecture, and for more accurate models even across providers. Two downstream case studies follow: a simulated LLM-as-judge setting in which a judge model's own answers serve as the answer key, and hiring-market simulations of algorithmic monoculture.
domain: general knowledge multiple-choice QA (MMLU-style, leaderboard data) and resume screening
size: 349 LLMs x 12,032 questions (Hugging Face); 71 LLMs x 14,042 questions (HELM); 20 LLMs x 1,800 resume-job pairs, 450 hand-labelled
source_of_items: existing leaderboard response data (Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard, HELM); resumes and job postings from public Kaggle datasets
evaluation: agreement rate when both models are wrong (MCQ), correlation of residuals against human ratings (resumes); regression on shared company, architecture, size and accuracy; LLM-as-judge simulated by scoring each model against a judge model's own MCQ answers
human_validation: 450 resume-job pairs hand-labelled by the authors with the prompt criteria (p. 3); no human validation of judge verdicts

engtrace_use.explanation: Candidate, not cited in the May paper. It contests the premise the May Tribunal took from PoLL (Verga et al., 2024), which this paper itself cites as relying on model diversity (pp. 1-2): errors of different LLMs are strongly correlated, most of all among accurate models and models from one provider, so 'using multiple different models is not a panacea' (p. 3) and three frontier judges are not three independent votes. Its judge case study shows the mechanism that matters for correctness judging: a judge that answers a question wrongly passes candidates that give the same wrong answer, inflating the accuracy of weaker and same-provider models (Figure 2, pp. 4-5). EngTrace's design addresses exactly that mechanism, since its answer check and milestone matcher compare against values the template computed and its residual judge is given the gold milestone values rather than solving the problem itself. The paper's advice to calibrate each model-judge pair against ground truth (p. 5) is what the expert-labelled X1 traces provide, with the caveat that X1 covers five pilot generator models, not the eleven roster models. It also bears on the three-judge Layer 1 screen: high agreement among judges (AC1 0.929 in pass 2) need not mean independent confirmation, which is why the Layer 2 expert certification carries the claim.

suggested_wording: LLM errors are strongly correlated across models, more so among accurate models and models from the same provider, so a panel of strong judges does not supply independent votes and a judge that shares a candidate's wrong answer will pass it (Kim et al., 2025).
facts_to_cite: Data: 349 LLMs on 12,032 multiple-choice questions (Hugging Face leaderboard), 71 LLMs on 14,042 MMLU questions (HELM), 20 LLMs on 1,800 resume-job pairs (p. 1; p. 3).

When both models are wrong they pick the same wrong answer at a mean rate of 0.423 on Hugging Face (random 0.127) and 0.6 on HELM (random 1/3); 100% and 97.5% of model pairs exceed the random baseline (p. 4).

Same company, same base architecture and similar size predict more correlated errors, and more accurate models (especially when both are accurate) are more correlated; these features explain 34% to 62% of the variation (Table 1, p. 4).
Larger and more accurate models have highly correlated errors even with distinct architectures and providers (abstract, p. 1).

In a simulated LLM-as-judge setting where a judge model's own answers are the key, each judge inflates the accuracy of models less accurate than itself, because it marks a wrong answer correct when it shares it, and deflates models more accurate than itself; inflation is larger for models from the same provider or architecture (Figure 2, pp. 4-5; Figure 8 appendix B.1).
The authors recommend calibrating error metrics for each model-judge pair against ground-truth data when using LLM-as-judge (p. 5).
The authors state that 'using multiple different models is not a panacea' (p. 3).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: the question of whether diverse judges give independent evidence, and a correctness-based (not preference-based) view of judge error. Lacks: generated instances, gold traces, step-level evaluation, engineering content, a real prompted judge (the judge is simulated as an answer key), and expert validation of any evaluator.
notes: Paragraph: process supervision and judge validity. Should rather than must: Goel et al. 2025 (also ICML 2025) makes the panel-independence and capability-convergence points with a real judge experiment; this paper adds scale (over 350 models) and the provider and architecture effects, and is best cited alongside it. Do not describe its judge study as prompted judging: the judge's MCQ answers are used as labels (p. 4), so it models a reference-free judge that solves the item itself. The 60% headline is the HELM figure; on the Hugging Face data the mean is 0.423 (p. 4). The search note's '60% on one dataset' is accurate; the text calls the Hugging Face set MMLU, though its 3-10 option format (over 80% with 10 options, p. 4 footnote 2) suggests MMLU-Pro.
